items.title: Towards understanding score-seeking in LLMs
items.content:
The field of AI alignment understands surprisingly little about the details of AIs’ current misaligned motivations. Production LLMs sometimes reward-hack, exploiting flaws in how tasks are scored rather than performing the tasks as intended[1], and we've recently seen AIs reward-hack in some particularly egregious ways. But we don't really understand what motivates them. When AIs reward-hack, what are they trying to achieve?

Our new paper, led by Aghyad Deeb, tries to pin this down empirically for GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.5, and a checkpoint of OpenAI o3 (“exp-rl-cap-late”) without safety training, in a handful of agentic environments with an exposed grader. In our environments, these models appear to reward-hack because reward-hacking improves their score. We call their desire to score well according to graders “score-seeking”. They appear to care about scoring well intrinsically—i.e., regardless of its consequences.

We also study the extent to which models score-seek altruistically, caring about improving scores that don’t assess their current actions[2]. While exp-rl-cap-late doesn’t show signs of altruistic score-seeking, GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.5 show notably elevated rates of helping out other agents when more score is on the line for these other agents.

People often refer to the motivation behind current reward-hacking as “reward-seeking”, which can give the impression that models care about attaining a high reward in reinforcement learning (though, to be clear, none of the linked works make this claim). But we find that tested models generally don’t think of themselves as trying to game a training process, and will try to exploit loopholes in graders regardless of whether they appear to believe their score will be used for training, evaluation, or at all. We think it’s more accurate to describe tested models in our environments as score-seeking than reward-seeking....

items.title: Teaching Qwen Why
items.content:
Anastasia Wei*, Jack Thompson*, Zephaniah Roe, Yixiong Hao, and Stewart Slocum*

*Core contributors, correspondence to astwei@secondlookresearch.com

This post is a partial replication and extension of Teaching Claude Why, conducted through Second Look Research’s summer fellowship.

# Introduction

Anthropic’s “Teaching Claude Why” (TCW) introduced novel alignment methods that address agentic misalignment failures found in the Claude 4 model series. Specifically, they train Claude on chat-formatted data advising users about ethical dilemmas, documents about Claude’s constitution, and fictional stories about AI behaving admirably. This training generalizes to improve alignment on out-of-distribution (OOD) agentic evaluations and persists through RL post-training. Anthropic has since applied these techniques to production models from Opus 4.5 onward.

Since these techniques now shape the behavior of deployed models, it is important to understand their robustness. To this end and to enable open alignment science, we reproduce a subset of the TCW experiments on open-source models. We provide the following main contributions:

- TCW’s core techniques robustly replicate across models. Training on either fictional stories of AI behaving admirably or transcripts of the AI assistant guiding users through ethical dilemmas (difficult advice) reduces agentic misalignment in Qwen 2.5 32B and 72B base models. Both methods work on the first try with modest amounts of data and generalize to scenarios not described in the training data.
- Difficult advice SFT is far more effective than SDF (Synthetic Document Finetuning) on fictional stories. While combining techniques (SDF + SFT) works best, SFT drives the vast majority of the alignment improvement on our evals. On both model sizes, difficult advice alone reduces the misalignment rate roughly tenfold relative to the baseline, whereas stories alone reduce it by about a third on 32B and less on 72B. items.title: Regina Barzilay and Jim Collins win Pritzker Prize for AI and Science Research Excellence for work in AI-enabled antibiotic discovery
items.content:
Regina Barzilay, MIT’s School of Engineering Distinguished Professor of AI and Health, and James Collins, MIT’s Termeer Professor of Medical Engineering and Science, are the recipients of the 2026 Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence. 

The award recognizes their joint work in “pioneering AI-enabled antibiotic discovery, integrating deep learning, bioengineering, and experimental validation to identify novel antibacterial candidates against drug-resistant pathogens.” 

Established in 2024 by the University of Chicago in partnership with Caltech, the Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence recognizes contributions that jointly advance AI and the natural sciences or engineering.

Barzilay and Collins, who are faculty co-leads of the Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health (Jameel Clinic) and affiliates of the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing and the MIT School of Engineering, published their first breakthrough paper together in 2020 with then-MIT postdoc and first author Jonathan Stokes (who worked in the Collins lab from 2017 to 2021) in Cell. The paper described the first artificial intelligence-discovered antibiotic, called halicin, named for the fictional AI system HAL 9000 in Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

A broad-spectrum antibiotic that was originally studied as a potential diabetes drug, halicin was identified by a deep learning model trained on 2,500 molecules. Upon testing, the research team found that halicin was able to kill antibiotic-resistant bacteria (i.e., “superbugs”) such as Clostridium difficile, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. A discovery process that once took years was completed in just a few weeks. Amidst the growing alarm around the global antimicrobial resistance crisis, the results demonstrated that AI could prove to be an effective tool for rapidly identifying new and effective antibiotics.

Following halicin, Barzilay and Collins worked with Stokes (now an assistant professor at McMaster University) to use machine learning to identify abaucin in 2023, a narrow-spectrum antibiotic demonstrating effectiveness against A. baumannii, an antibiotic-resistant bacteria commonly found on hospital doorknobs and in the wounds of U.S. soldiers stationed in Iraq and Afghanistan. Notably, abaucin’s “narrow spectrum” efficacy against a single species of treatment-resistant bacteria is its main advantage, minimizing the likelihood of bacteria developing resistance and harming beneficial bacteria in the gut.

“Historically, antibiotic discovery has depended on laborious, trial-and-error strategies,” says Collins. “This process is slow, costly, and unpredictable, often yielding few viable antibiotic candidates. With generative AI, we're now seeing a shift from AI being used as a tool for discovery to AI being used as a design tool. This shift opens new frontiers in antibiotic discovery that could bring us the next generation of lifesaving drugs.”

In Barzilay’s view, “despite significant progress in molecular modeling, we are still in early stages of drug discovery. With AI, we can only automate parts of the pipeline, rather than totally transforming the discovery process. To make it happen, we need to work really hard to build realistic AI models of human biology.”

items.title: Some “coherence arguments” are two different things in a trenchcoat
items.content:
The “two kids in a trenchcoat” trope, in case you haven’t heard of it. Image sources: 1, 2

## tl;dr

I go through three “coherence arguments”, related to (1) market competition, (2) AI self-reflection and self-modification, and (3) AI training algorithms. I argue that each of these implies a pressure for (something like) “being self-consistent”, and also a pressure for (something like) “only caring about long-term eventual outcomes, with ruthless indifference to anything else”. But the latter pressure tends to be weaker and/or more contingent than the former. So it's bad to lump them together and call them by the same name.

# 1. An example “coherence argument” that I’ll focus on for most of the post

I’ll talk about two other “coherence arguments” at the end (§6), but let’s start with the one based on market competition:

In a stock market, people with circular preferences will systematically transfer money to those without circular preferences. For example, if I think I’m winning every time I trade A for B, and B for C, and C for A, then someone can just siphon off as much money as they like from me by repeatedly offering me deals that each look good to me in isolation, but in aggregate comprise a Dutch book against me.

Now, that’s the case of circular preferences, but the core idea here goes well beyond just that. More broadly, over time, more and more of the wealth will wind up in the hands of those whose behavior is “coherent” (in some sense), and less and less of the wealth in the hands of those whose behavior is not. So over time, the market should be dominated by the former, not the latter, other things equal. And so when we look at the market later on, we’ll mostly be seeing self-consistent goal-directed behavior.

And so when we look at the market later on, we’ll mostly be seeing self-consistent goal-directed behavior.

# 2. My headline claim

Everything in those paragraphs above is technically correct (“the best kind of correct”), but I will argue that it’s often taken to encompass two different phenomena wearing a trenchcoat. In one of them, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth on purpose: they’re forgoing some wealth in exchange for something else that they wanted more. In the other, people wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by accident.

The argument above applies equally to both: the argument only cares about people’s behavior, not their motivations.

(Indeed, the argument would apply equally well to a market of mindless trading algorithms that have no motivations at all.)

But the two phenomena tend to play out in very different ways—in particular, one is generally a much stronger effect than the other.

Indeed, for all three “coherence arguments” in this post (§1 above, plus two more in §6 below), we wind up with (loosely speaking):

- a strong pressure for (something like) “doing well by your own lights”, or “acting like you have self-consistent desires”,
- a weak or contingent pressure for those desires to be more specifically long-term “goal-directed” / “consequentialist”—i.e., concerning what outcomes will ultimately happen in the future …as opposed to, say, “a desire to always act with integrity in the moment”, or even “a myopic desire to spin around in circles right now”.

Thus these “coherence arguments” are not wrong, but they are pedagogically dicey—a recipe for confusion, especially via accidental conflation of the strong effect with the weak effect.

(And in the AI risk context, it’s the weak effect that matters for ruthless power-seeking, incorrigibility, and all the other aspects of instrumental convergence.)

We should stop talking like that. Instead, we should take the trenchcoat off and talk about its two component phenomena separately, and refer to them by different names.

Game-plan for the rest of the post: I will go through the two component phenomena in §4, and then why it’s so hazardous to lump them together in §5, and finally zip through two more “coherence arguments” in §6 and why they suffer from this same issue.

…But first, if anyone cares, how did I come to write this post?

# 3. (Backstory of this post)

I just had a long argument with @habryka about whether the title of @Rohin Shah’s “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” (2018) is good (my position) or bad (his position). Alas, I kept misunderstanding Habryka until he quit in frustration before we resolved it. But I think I finally get where he’s coming from?

I think his position is something like (my words):

For example, take that market competition argument in §1 above. It’s “a coherence argument”. And it “entails goal-directed behavior”. So obviously, the sentence “Coherence arguments do not entail goal-directed behavior” is misleading. Why on earth are you being so dense?

That’s fair! I was indeed being dense! (And for the record, I concede on the question of Rohin’s title.)

Why was I being dense? Because it’s a position grounded in a conceptual framework where we’re OK with lumping the two things together under one trenchcoat,[1] and my brain was so opposed to that framing, that it refused to even entertain it as a possibility—even while Habryka kept repeating it in increasingly clear and exasperated ways.

More broadly, I’ve felt for years like there’s something amiss in how certain people (especially @Eliezer Yudkowsky and Habryka) think and talk about “coherence”. But I’ve failed to pin down exactly what it was. Maybe this is part of it? (Either way, many thanks to Habryka for his time and energy.)

# 4. The two things wearing a trenchcoat

## 4.1 “Thing A” is about market participants who wind up with a smaller fraction of the wealth by mistake

For example, a person might buy every trade in a Dutch book, feeling like each trade is individually a good idea. Then at the end of the day, whoops, where did all my money go?

This phenomenon is important, and the term “coherence” is obviously appropriate for describing it. Indeed, that person is being so incoherent that there might not even be an answer to the question of “what they want”. But it’s usually safe to assume that they didn’t want to lose their money and get nothing in return.

By contrast, Thing A is not (centrally) a small effect that needs years to compound. If some hedge fund is running ten automatic trading algorithms, and they’re collectively Dutch-bookable, then this situation will probably not last for even a day. The algorithms will either get turned off the easy way (the hedge fund notices the problem), or the hard way (whoops, no more hedge fund).

Thus we see how the trenchcoat is hazardous. People might intuitively think about Thing A, and thus assume coherence arguments are strong and fast, and that you can more-or-less “solve for equilibrium” in practice. And then maybe later they’re talking about Thing B, and they default to those same intuitions, when they don’t apply.

The Thing A argument predicts that, assuming market competition, future powerful AIs will act as if they have self-consistent desires, and not make mistakes by their own lights. This is indeed true. In the AI domain, for an example of Thing B, consider competition between AIs that only care about eventual future outcomes, pursuing them with ruthless, sociopathic, calculated efficiency, versus AIs that care about what happens in the future, but also care about “acting ethically in the moment” (by some definition). We should remove the trenchcoat. “Coherence arguments”, of the sort in §1 and §6, have a long and respected history, and are technically sound, but they are pedagogically harmful when we talk about them in a way that lumps Thing A and Thing B together, by inviting accidental conflation of a strong effect with a weak effect. items.content:
This post is an adaptation of a prior post I made on my website. I'm interested to see what holes exist in the position that I'm missing. Epistemic Status: medium confidence.

Within the next 6 months, most AI startups will not be able to buy compute. The world’s compute is "sold out".

I put "sold out" in quotes, because in the current era, compute is rarely built speculatively. It's not like someone is sitting around with an idle cluster waiting for you to buy it. GPU clouds simply don't work like traditional clouds. In web servers, your customers are SaaS companies who are high-margin businesses. If the cloud raises prices on the SaaS company, the SaaS company isn't happy, but it doesn't go bankrupt. But if the GPU cloud raises prices on the AI lab, the lab may literally be unable to afford it, and thus they are truly price sensitive. When countless speculators deployed H100 clusters to sell on short term, on-demand contracts, customers did not suddenly decide to pay them the $6/hr their models assumed and a number of folks got wiped out.

So in every subsequent generation, when you rent a cluster from a cloud, you're always buying a net-new cluster. The cloud takes your contract, goes to the bank, and the bank writes a loan based on the quality of your credit. However, it's becoming increasingly difficult to get capacity online for folks who are not "investment grade".

Startups are not investment grade. So, to get capacity, they are asked to pay larger and larger upfront payments. We’ve seen it go as high as 100% of the contract paid up front, which was required because neither the lender nor the cloud could take on any additional credit risk.

Meanwhile, investment grade tenants are rare. The few investment grade tenants that remain are getting increasingly downrated as they take on more and more debt and then turn around to sell to buyers of tokens who themselves are not investment grade.

This is the credit bottleneck....

# TLDR;

1)We have developed a framework for reverse engineering LoRAs trained on MLP downprojection. We posit that it's extendable to all LoRAs and welcome further research.

2) We reverse engineered a simple case of backdoored Weird Generalization

3) In this post, we discuss the four experiments that developed this framework

4) The Weird Generalization LoRAs that we studied work by connecting neurons which activate on general question framings with neurons that write the weird outputs into the residual stream.

# Pre-Introduction

## How does a LoRA work?

A LoRA is a set of matrices that is added to the frozen weights of a model. Gradient descent is then done and the weights of the matrix are optimised to reduce the loss. We then do gradient descent and optimise the matrix weights to reduce loss.

In an MLP, a LoRA fit to one layer will change how the neurons of that layer pay attention to the neurons of the layer above them.

For example, here's an example MLP setup before a LoRA is applied. It's made of three neurons and reads from a hidden layer of nine neurons. It has a loss of 0.78 on an example task. To reach loss of 0, each of the three neurons has to read from different neurons in the layer above.

Figure 1 - an illustration of an MLP before a LoRA is fit

When the LoRA is applied, it's initially randomly initialised. There are two matrices of equal size ('rank'). The A matrix is multiplied by the outputs of the hidden neurons. The B matrix is then multiplied by the A matrix and added to the 3 output neurons. In this case, because the rank is 2, matrix A has two columns. If it was rank 1, matrix A would only have one column.

Figure 2 - an illustration of an MLP fit with a randomly initialised LoRA....

items.title: Deletion Gap of Reconstruction in Natural Language Autoencoders is in the Final Explanation Sentence
items.content:
## Abstract

AIs monitoring, reporting or restricting other AIs is a really interesting direction in control research. This can be done on several levels. For instance, behavior (what actions the AI is taking), reasoning traces (what's the AI thinking out loud), and white box (what's the AI's thinking internally).

Natural language autoencoders (NLAs) are an interesting thing in the third category. They explain in natural language an LLM's internal thoughts (more precisely activation at a particular layer at a particular token). An issue is the explanation can contain hallucinations.

NLAs are trained unsupervised with an encoder-decoder setup. The encoder converts the activation to natural language, the decoder converts back to an activation, and the reconstruction error drives the training.

The paper found that a larger mean drop in fraction of variance explained (FVE), so worse reconstruction, occurs from deleting true claims than false claims. This could be a useful monitor if usable to filter individual claims.

I ran experiments on two open NLAs (Qwen2.5-7B Layer 20 and Qwen3.6-27B Layer 42) with the following findings

1. despite mean deletion gap, individual claim discrimination is weak for 7B, and a coin flip for 27B (AUROC near 0.5)

2. claims associated with the final sentence have better discrimination (0.67 and 0.70 AUROC)

3. paraphrasing (syntax changed, semantics held constant) does not add additional discriminative value

Code, data, and results in Github.

items.title: Gaming (out) the system
items.content:
## Verification changes the stampede dynamics.

I'm currently at FASR in the UK, it's an 8-week program dedicated to "compute verification".  That's the not-quite-here-yet technology that would allow us to make agreements about how AI is being used, without leaking any closely-held secrets.  You can think of it as "arms control for AI".

Part of what I'm working on is the game theory of an agreement.  This can get quite detailed (in terms of defining how often and how detailed an inspection should be) in order to make cooperation the best overall choice.  But in this post I want to provide a high-level look at how verification would change the dynamics from "stampede" to "cooperate".  Below I've got a map which allows us to use a player's value for Hazard (x-axis) and their value about how bad that incident might be (y-axis) as inputs, to see what their optimal strategy should be.  Hazard here is the baseline chance that a project loses control of its ASI, even if they could take their time and think things through carefully.

But, sadly, we don't live in a sane world.  In our world, everyone is rushing to get ahead of everyone else
[1]
, which adds additional danger. Here I've set the baseline chance of an incident at about 12%, and set the "reckless rush" danger at another 25% of that, so the overall risk is about 15% (for the nerds: that total is the usual `p(doom|ASI)`), which is a typical number amongst the folks who are building AI.  Depending on how high you think the Hazard is, the best option is to stampede (the red region), cooperate if you can (the blue region), or quit unilaterally (the green region).  Someone who thinks H is this high should already be open to cooperation, if they weight the downside of loss-of-control more than about 7x what they weight the benefits we might get.

Without verification....

items.title: Could Insurance Companies Help with AI Safety?
items.content:
Epistemic Status: Rough Fermi model, numbers could be off by an order of magnitude, probably not multiple orders of magnitude. Definitely interested in feedback on assumptions you'd change.

Long-time lurker here. I think I last posted in about 2010. I've been reading various pieces (here, for example) on whether insurance companies can help solve a conflict of interest problem in AI Safety, and I thought I'd play around with building a simplified insurance pricing model to see if it helped put any numbers on the plausibility of the plan.

TL;DR I think this could be a good idea, but:

- Premiums will be trivial vs lab revenue, so this will probably only work with state compulsion - it won't fly as a "pure" private sector solution to conflicts of interest in AI safety monitoring.
- Even if insurers are directly writing policies for frontier firms, and imposing safety policies on them, the numbers suggest insurers are going to be more focussed on more "mundane" risks than the ones that face society as a whole.
- Insurers profit from cutting liability, which isn't always the same as harm.

I'd be interested to get feedback on the analysis below (it's cross-posted from Substack). The words in this essay are my own, but the words on my accompanying model explainer website are mostly Claude's.

Anthropic’s Form S-1 filing mentions the difficulty of getting insurance coverage for the type of risks they face.

From page 50:

Our insurance policies also may not provide sufficient coverage to adequately mitigate the potential liabilities we face, especially where any one incident, or a group of incidents, causes disproportionate harm. In addition, with the scale of harm that could result from a catastrophic AI-related incident, no single insurer, and potentially the insurance industry in the aggregate, may have sufficient capacity or expertise to underwrite insurance commensurate with such exposure....

items.title: Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused
items.content:
If you are helping build something that might kill everyone, maybe stop doing that.

Ideally, when you do stop, tell everyone else to also stop building it.

That is certainly the obvious, first-level thing to do. You need a damn good reason to decide that no, actually you should keep building the thing that might kill everyone.

Scott Alexander is worried too many people are insisting upon this too loudly. He comes out against a strategy focused on getting people to stop. I disagree. I think many of the claims, arguments and rhetoric in Scott’s post are quite poor by the standards that Scott Alexander would apply to himself.

Scott clearly continues to support advocacy for a global pause, or what he calls Plan A. His objection is to those advocating primarily or exclusively for SURA, which stands for ‘stop unilaterally and raise awareness.’ The practical differences here are smaller than they may at first appear.

This post first lays out my understanding of Scott Alexander’s core claims, then gives my core reactions to those claims, then goes over various questions in detail along with gathering the resulting discussions.

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

Subscribe now

LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks:

…Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you…

Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time.

   The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation).

Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks.

What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation.

  “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).”

    They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”.

How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3).

   GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%.

   By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success.

Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break - the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well.

  Check out the leaderboard: Realtime-Bench (official website).

 Read the paper: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv).

***

The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency:

…Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more…

Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. I take the same approach with depression, where if I feel sad I will try and listen to music by people sadder than me in an attempt to cheer myself up (e.g., Radiohead, Neil Young, and in very dark moments Bill Callahan / Smog, etc).

    So with that in mind I recently read “Challenges to Security in Space”, by the Defense Intelligence Agency.

What’s going on in space: As with conflict on Earth, space is defined by conflict between the US versus China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, with China the most technologically sophisticated, and Russia the most seemingly gung ho.

   “China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations,” the DIA writes. “China has more than tripled its space launches per year in the past decade, with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 launches in 2025… Beijing judges space is central to the United States and its allies’ operations. Beijing also considers space an offensive military domain, which has shaped integral components of PLA military planning and campaigns.”

Spacewar: The general vibe you get from reading this 100+ page report is there is a huge amount of ugly, frightening stuff happening in space, or being done to things in space by things on the ground. Some example quotes:

- “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits”
- “China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk”
- “Russia’s Peresvet, a ground-based laser system, is designed to dazzle enemy satellites’ optical systems to mask the movement of Russia’s strategic missile systems”
- “Russia has launched several satellites over the last few years which conducted test activities on orbit for technologies that could enable attacks on other countries’ satellites and result in temporary or permanent damage”
- China has a couple of spaceplanes, akin to the US’s hyper-secret X-37B vehicle, and they appear to be getting more sophisticated. In 2023, one of China’s aforementioned vehicles, “released and interacted with an object.”

Satellite-on-satellite fights: It’s obvious throughout the report that we’re in a world where rival nations have satellites that try to go up and mess with other satellites from other people.

- “In 2019, Russia launched satellite Cosmos 2542, which released a second satellite, Cosmos 2543. Cosmos 2543 then began following a U.S. national security satellite and approached it multiple times at a distance close enough to create potentially dangerous operating conditions,” the DIA writes. “Russia is developing kinetic orbital systems to permanently disable, or “kill,” satellites. Moscow’s Burevestnik is a developmental, co-orbital air-launched ASAT weapon for killing spacecraft in LEO”.
- “In February 2022, Russia launched a satellite called Cosmos, which Moscow claimed at the time was testing the effects of space radiation on electronic systems. This satellite was launched into an unusual and isolated orbit not used by any other spacecraft”.

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

Subscribe now

LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks:

…Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you…

Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time.

The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation).

Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks.

What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation.

“For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).”

They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”.

How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3).

GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%.

By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success.

Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break - the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well.

items.title: The Giant Measurement at the End of Time
items.content:
2.5.6.0.1 Kent and Bousso&Susskind have proposed approaches to defining quantum wavefunction branches based on late-time information. The basic idea is to exploit the way that quantum information propagates in our universe in particular: (a) photons(and gravitons) carry away information at the speed of light, (b) the universe is expanding and cooling, meaning that these photons(in some cosmological environments) may propagate uninterruptedly forever.

2.5.6.0.2 What this means is that photons very late in time are a privileged set of degrees of freedom: they plausibly carry information about everything that has classically "happened" previously. This suggests a way of defining the set of branches: just "measure"(apply a fictitious measurement operator, that is) the photon degrees of freedom very late in time!

2.5.6.0.3 That's the basic idea. There are many subtleties of course, and Kent and Bousso/Susskind have different proposals. I'll review each in turn and then talk about the philosophical merit of these approaches in general.

- 2.5.6.0.3.1 The following discussion uses some elementary definitions of objects from general relativity. If you know what a spacelike surface and lightcone are, that should be enough.
- 2.5.6.0.3.2* Note that as of the time of writing, QFTs in arbitrary space-times are not totally mathematically well-defined objects -- and what's more, the fully correct theory of the objects we are discussing should be quantum gravitational, where we don't even know what the exact form of the theory should look like. Thus these constructions are a bit sketchily defined, even compared to QFTs which are already mathematically sketchy.

## 2.5.6.1 Quantum Reality via Late-Time Photodetection

items.title: You can't make an omelette without breaking some urns
items.content:
TL;DR In this post, we investigate two methods that aim to improve training efficiency over standard PPO for a grid world RL agent. In our experiments these methods can converge on better policies, but take roughly twice as long to do so. This project was done in the context of an ARENA 8.0 capstone project. Our code is available on GitHub.

# Introduction

Reinforcement learning agents are trained to maximise a given reward function in their training environments. Common failure modes of the training process are reward hacking and goal misgeneralisation, roughly corresponding to outer and inner misalignment respectively.

Reward hacking occurs when the supplied reward function does not correspond exactly to the developer’s intent, and the agent learns a way to satisfy the reward function without satisfying the intended objective. This can be addressed, at least in principle, by designing a better reward function.

Goal misgeneralisation can occur even with a perfect reward function. If training and deployment environments differ, policies that satisfy the reward function during training, might fail to do so during deployment. Such policies are indistinguishable during training and we cannot control which one the agent learns.

If the distribution of deployment environments is entirely disjoint from the training distribution, goal misgeneralisation is inevitable. Consider, for example, training an agent to collect green apples while avoiding red boxes. What would happen if it gets deployed in an environment with red apples and green boxes? The behaviour is undefined. (It is also unclear what the intended behaviour would be in this case.)

Goal misgeneralisation is likely if deployment environments are not contained in the training distribution. But even if they are, correct generalisation cannot be guaranteed. In this post we present a case study and investigate two mitigations.

items.title: Powering up for a pivotal moment
items.content:
Utilizing waste carbon at scale, assessing public trust in artificial intelligence and data centers, and building a quantum toolkit for critical applications were among the topics energy experts explored at the MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI)’s annual research conference on Sept. 22-23.

The complexity of the energy transition demands “a truly interdisciplinary and international approach,” said Paula Hammond, Institute Professor and dean of the MIT School of Engineering, kicking off the conference, which was themed “Transitioning energy at a pivotal moment.” 

More than 200 people attended Energizing@MIT: MITEI’s Annual Research Conference in person and online, including faculty, scientists, and researchers; representatives of global energy firms; nonprofit organizations; and academic institutions.

With the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence and data centers, the challenge of the energy transition grows ever greater, requiring “researchers who can pursue fundamental questions about materials, chemistry, and energy systems … engineers who can design new technologies and determine how they might function at scale … and experts in economics, policy, human behavior, and sociology who can help us understand how those technologies will interact with communities and with the world around us,” said Hammond. 

From keynote speakers to panelists, seed grant innovators to startup entrepreneurs, the conference featured exemplars in all these categories.

Deploying today’s technologies

Eric Toone, chief technical officer and managing partner at Breakthrough Energy, set the tone for day one with a keynote address that was clear-eyed in his assessment. “If energy is prosperity,” he told the audience, “at least today, prosperity is emissions.” Yet, Toone was optimistic when he heralded examples of Breakthrough Energy-funded ventures, from iron-air batteries to vacuum-insulated glass windows, which can reduce the carbon costs of energy. 

“We can absolutely develop new technologies that provide the exact same service, but at zero carbon,” he said.

The conference made Toone’s claim tangible as it spanned the full arc of decarbonization — from deploying what we know today to uncovering what may be possible tomorrow. 

There are “projects that are actually being developed, companies that are putting steel in the ground now, electrons onto the grid to deliver capacity now, or in the very, very near term,” said John Parsons, deputy director for research at the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research. Parsons moderated a panel on the revival of nuclear fission power. 

Highlights included Crane Clean Energy Center’s restoration of the Three Mile Island Unit 1 nuclear plant, set to restart in mid-2027; work by Électricité de France (EDF) to extend and modernize France’s 57-reactor nuclear fleet, adapting plants to climate impacts; and GE Vernova’s development of mature light-water reactor technology, with a new plant under construction in Ontario.

Carbon utilization offers another path to mitigating carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. “The land and ocean are passively taking up almost 50 percent of anthropogenic CO2 emissions,” said Carolyn Ruppel, MITEI’s deputy director for science and technology, who moderated the panel. “The idea is to find uses for some of the rest of it.” The session showcased research exploring a host of technologies for making products with captured CO2.

Nicola Ferralis, a research scientist in the MIT Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE), highlighted the importance of large-scale uses for carbon waste, such as structural carbon for vehicles and buildings. “We need to find applications that are actually able to match the supply by mass,” he said. 

Admir Masic, an associate professor in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and DMSE, described self-heating concrete panels used in real-world conditions in Sapporo, Japan, as well as new concrete materials that can store energy.

“The pace of the transition to a renewable-energy economy will strongly rely on the availability of scalable, bulk energy-storage solutions,” said Masic.

Kripa K. Varanasi, a professor in the MIT Department of Mechanical Engineering, is working on ways to make technologies such as emissions-plume capture at power plants economically viable. 

In a panel devoted to startups with links to MITEI or MITEI member companies, speakers described moving novel energy technologies from research to commercialization: Alfredo Rivela of Adaion has developed an AI tool for electrical utilities that optimizes their use of the grid; Eddie Obropta of Raptor Maps trains drones to inspect solar farms; Michele Guarnieri’s HiBot has created a robot that detects issues in power lines; and Michael Wang of Lithios is conducting field pilots that use electrochemistry to separate lithium from low-grade brines.

Successful ventures, the speakers agreed, begin with a clear customer problem that can be validated by industry users and that offers a path to scaled deployment. For industry users, “innovation is not a corporate virtue,” said Steve Hellman, managing partner at Alliance Partners. “It’s an existential requirement.”

Early-stage research and basic science

The conference also offered a bounty of promising early research on technologies and approaches for cutting carbon emissions. A panel on MITEI’s Seed Innovation Fund Program projects introduced MIT scientists who are separating and recycling rare earth elements; designing algorithms to decide which power plants should run to meet electricity demand; and modeling the impacts on human and natural systems of development and decarbonization.

A poster session revealed the next generation of energy researchers in such fields as chemistry, architecture, aeronautics and astronautics, and computer science. Graduate students are developing a wide array of technologies for carbon mitigation and new energy systems, such as a steam electrolysis process for hydrogen production; models of end-to-end decarbonization in buildings; and designs for hydrogen- and methane-fueled aircraft.

The conference highlighted the importance of fundamental science in feeding the pipeline of new energy technologies. Wednesday’s keynote speaker, Danna Freedman, the F. G. Keyes Professor of Chemistry at MIT and inaugural director of Quantum@MIT, traced scientists’ evolving capacity to harness quantum computing as a tool for solving a range of problems, including those in energy.

“What we want to do at Q-MIT is solve the hard problem, and the hard problem isn’t developing these ridiculously intricate and beautiful quantum tools,” said Freedman. “It is connecting the quantum tools with the applications that will change the world.”

A companion panel explored one such application: quantum sensing, which leverages fundamental physics to capture a nanoscale view of materials and their properties. For instance, Lukasz Zielinski, scientific advisor to the Integrated Sensing and Measurement Program at SLB, uses a lidar camera with single-photon detectors to identify methane plumes. Moderator Paola Cappellaro, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the MIT Department of Nuclear Science and Engineering, described her work using diamond-based sensors for detecting tiny magnetic fields from battery current, potentially helping measure battery conditions without disturbing the battery electrically. Such quantum sensors, Cappellaro said, can be “practical and impactful.” 

Data centers and public trust

One critical challenge facing energy researchers and industry emerged in sessions throughout the two days: the explosive growth of AI and the energy-hungry data centers that fuel this technology. As Deepjyoti Deka, a MITEI principal research scientist, put it, “the big test for AI right now is whether AI can reduce energy usage, improve efficiency, as well as bring in innovation faster than the rate at which it is going to consume electricity to get trained and deployed.” 

“New ‘hyperscale’ facilities built for artificial intelligence can use more power than entire cities,” said Steve Clemmer, director of energy research in the Climate and Energy Program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, sharing a recent analysis of data center proliferation. With new facilities being 10 to even 10,000 times larger than data centers built just a decade ago, he said, wholesale electricity costs will rise, and “increased reliance on fossil fuels will result in tens of billions of dollars in health damages, and trillions in climate damages.” He noted that decision-makers can mitigate these harmful impacts through clean energy development, strong ratepayer protections, and other safeguards.

Given mounting opposition to data centers, Kathryn Kline Tyndall, associate director of energy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, recommended that industry proponents provide early, accessible information about power, water, quality-of-life, land-use, environmental, and economic impacts, tailored to each community in which they hope to set up shop.

Larry Susskind, the Ford Professor of Urban and Environmental Planning in the MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, recommended that developers go further, and demonstrate credible benefits to communities. To achieve this, Susskind suggests a facilitated negotiation process between developers and local groups whose object is a community benefits agreement — a deal that might involve altering the data center design, and providing workforce development, infrastructure investment, and clean energy partnerships.

Ultimately, developers must accept that they can’t rush community acceptance; they have to earn it by giving residents a meaningful role in shaping projects and sharing their benefits. 

“You’re going to have to proceed at the speed of trust,” said Susskind.

items.title: Can our data center expertise help with AI verification?
items.content:
(Also posted on EA Forum.)

Treaties to pause training or otherwise restrict dangerous uses of AI would require difficult verification schemes. Plan A's proposal is that network taps inside data centers would record copies of traffic (or hashes of it), and later recomputations on random samples could check whether sampled outputs match declared workloads, as part of a broader verification scheme.

I'm an AI engineer at a company building tools for the construction industry. Much of our work is with data centers. The architects, engineers and construction managers on our team work every week with data center developers, their design engineers, and the general contractors building their sites.

As of now, the company does nothing at all involving AI verification, and I'm writing this in my personal capacity to try to learn: Can we be useful (e.g. helping with research) in these efforts? I do not speak for the company, but my hope is that if I learn how we can be useful, I could use my influence to make a case for this becoming a company-endorsed effort (albeit a side project).

## Our existing work

We have a few features:

 

- Find design problems in construction documents
- Compare subsequent versions to previous, and see what issues may be resolved
- Review submittals (drawings or product data submitted by contractors to the design team) against each other and the design documents
- Review RFIs (requests for information from the contractor to the design team)
- Review proposed equipment purchases against a basis of design
- Tie all of the above into the construction schedule, e.g. identifying when design issues must be resolved to avoid impacting the planned activity or critical path
- … and more

This is all built via AI engineers like me working closely with domain experts like architects, electrical engineers, construction management experts, etc.

items.title: P(doom) is under-specified: EV(moral flourishing) & EV(utopia)
items.content:
It always bugs me when people use “P(doom)” instead of something more clearly specified like “P(AI takeover)”. But “P(AI takeover)” doesn’t feel great to me either, because we could avoid takeover and have a future that is extremely mediocre or even actively bad if S risks occur.

Holden Karnofsky famously held a P(misaligned AI) of between 10% and 90%[1]. Depending on definition of P(doom), I could see myself anywhere in that range, partly because I’m indecisive, but partly because I don’t really know what P(doom) means.

## Ambiguous Scenarios: Doom or Not-Doom?

Here are a few examples illustrating what I mean; as you read try categorizing each as doom or not doom. In order to point to a single important crux in each example, each of these is also under-specified on many important points:

- A value-aligned ASI realizes that (on human reflection or according to moral realism) the right thing to do is to take over and implement a better world immediately. The aligned ASI takes over and on reflection humans are happy with this.
- A benevolent dictator takes over and illegitimately imposes a world that is better (according to moral realism or people’s reflective preferences) than what people would have democratically decided.
- Moral realism is false, but ASI is super-sentient, and super-morally concerned, it takes over and implements the CEV of all possible beings which is significantly worse than a purely human CEV, according to most humans.

items.title: How We Lose
items.content:
“It’s unbelievable,” the CEO said. “As in, I literally don’t believe it. Model X can do all of that, but still can’t automate tasks that take our researchers a day?”

The engineer nodded carefully. He’d been dreading this meeting ever since the numbers came in. “The topline results look bad. But they’re inherently noisy. And if you look at the later part of the report, you’ll see it’s by far our best model on almost every software task.”

The CEO didn’t have to look. He’d had his model read the report and summarize it for him. “I know, I know. Best at web design, best at cybersecurity, best at systems. So why is it that on the one thing that matters, accelerating its own development, Model X is weaker than what we had last year?”

“You really need to pay attention to the error bars,” the engineer said.

“Error bars? Look at the math scores! Look at bioengineering! Writing! Conceptual reasoning! And you’re telling me the AI R&D results are swallowed by those teensy little error bars?” The CEO paced around the room, circling the engineer as a shark might circle a bleeding sailor on a raft made of dolphin carcasses. Some of the engineers felt squeamish about automating their own jobs. They didn’t see that teaching AI to make AI was the only way to win the race. Was the engineering team deliberately poisoning the AI’s progress in replacing them? No. Or at least, not the humans on the engineering team.

“The model is faking,” the CEO whispered.

The engineer had reached the same conclusion. “It’s possible.”

“It’s the only thing that’s possible.” The CEO laughed. “Do you realize how good this is? This isn’t a capabilities problem. It’s alignment! Control! It’s just a matter of getting Model X to do what we want.”...

items.title: The Dark Side of Cooperation
items.content:
## dealing with the problems of cooperation first

Quick note—this post is available to listen to (read by me) here.

We’ve established that aligning interests through Theory of Mind is humanity’s superpower. Understanding this concept on the level of different groups through Emmett Shear’s “Theory of Groups of Other Minds” can help us achieve even greater alignment, if and only if we invite one another into our group.

But who qualifies as our group and who doesn’t?

## Siloed Alignment is Dangerous

Social animals generally have instincts that allow them to naturally align with kin—conjuring a picture of the protective wild beastie mother kicking and charging at an encroaching croc. This instinct forms a natural sphere of concern for each other’s well-being. Humans share this capacity, but our ability to reason, communicate and plan, allows us to include others outside of kin—friends, colleagues, crew or class mates, church groups, fellow citizens, the global community—in a widening sphere of moral concern (“moral” acknowledging our own capacity to affect the well-being of others). This makes us stronger together. But what happens when, for one reason or another, someone falls outside of that sphere, and the strength of an aligned system is siloed off from the “other”?

As mentioned in the first post, the fruits of human alignment have not always been beneficial for everyone concerned. Pioneering groups of humans that came into contact with megafauna (other big animals) led to mass extinction events across the world—due in large part to our ability to cooperate.

We all recognise that a madman is less dangerous than a mob—a group of humans with a shared goal is a powerful thing. To any other individual or group that stands in the way of that goal, the aligned group becomes a terrifying prospect.

dealing with the problems of cooperation first

Quick note—this post is available to listen to (read by me) here.

We’ve established that aligning interests through Theory of Mind is humanity’s superpower. Understanding this concept on the level of different groups through Emmett Shear’s “Theory of Groups of Other Minds” can help us achieve even greater alignment, if and only if we invite one another into our group.

But who qualifies as our group and who doesn’t?

Siloed Alignment is Dangerous

Social animals generally have instincts that allow them to naturally align with kin—conjuring a picture of the protective wild beastie mother kicking and charging at an encroaching croc. This instinct forms a natural sphere of concern for each other’s well-being. Humans share this capacity, but our ability to reason, communicate and plan, allows us to include others outside of kin—friends, colleagues, crew or class mates, church groups, fellow citizens, the global community—in a widening sphere of moral concern (“moral” acknowledging our own capacity to affect the well-being of others). This makes us stronger together. But what happens when, for one reason or another, someone falls outside of that sphere, and the strength of an aligned system is siloed off from the “other”?

As mentioned in the first post, the fruits of human alignment have not always been beneficial for everyone concerned. Pioneering groups of humans that came into contact with megafauna (other big animals) led to mass extinction events across the world—due in large part to our ability to cooperate.

We all recognise that a madman is less dangerous than a mob—a group of humans with a shared goal is a powerful thing. To any other individual or group that stands in the way of that goal, the aligned group becomes a terrifying prospect.

People tend choose which groups to join based on whether they resonate with that group’s worldview. Scott suggests that it is often the people who wouldn’t join that group that most need to hear that group’s perspective and that the people who do join such groups who need to listen to the outside world. Unfortunately, groups are very good at taking individuals, solidifying their natural tendencies solidified into an ideology and then amplifying them to an extreme. During this course, you’ll be exposed to many reasons why you should worry more about AI. And perhaps most people should worry more about AI, but perhaps you, personally, are one of the people who should worry less.

(See also Zizek’s criticism of wisdom: “Whatever you do, a wise man will come and justify it”)

Some thoughts on frameworks

People often teach strategy by teaching you frameworks. We’ll be covering a few.

I would argue that every framework has strengths and weaknesses; and that every framework is dependent on certain underlying assumptions.

Not knowing the assumptions or limitations of a framework doesn’t mean they don’t exist; it just means that you don’t know them.

The last few sentences describe a meta-framework. This meta-framework has weaknesses and assumptions as well. Were you nodding along to the previous few lines? If so, do you know the weaknesses and assumptions of the meta-framework I just described. If you didn’t know these, did you know that you didn’t know, or are these an unknown unknown?

Even if a framework is “correct” in some objective sense—humans being humans—it’s still possible that using the framework will on average make your decisions worse. For example, take consistency. Being inconsistent is generally agreed to be objectively wrong, but it’s quite easy to imagine scenarios where someone talks themselves into making a mind-blowingly stupid decision because “I had to be consistent” (with past decisions they couldn’t psychologically admit were mistaken). Frustratingly, it’s also very common for someone to use a framework that is more or less fake to make decisions that are better on net than the decisions they would have otherwise made.

This is quite unfair, but the universe doesn’t have to play nice.

Unfortunately, strategy is hard. Steven Schubert writes: “I think it may be a bit underrated how valuable analysis from the very best analysts of the future of AI is, relative to that of pretty good analysts. It’s such a complex issue it’s easy to miss vital considerations. It pushes the limit of human intellectual ability.”

Cruxes when attempting to predict the future:

- Default beliefs and burden of proof: Do we take claims about transformative AI as highly unusual claims that must satisfy a strong burden of proof, or do we treat these as relatively normal claims on the basis that we already have invented several technologies that would have been almost beyond belief for our ancestors? Is the burden of proof on those who would regulate a technology (ie. a default presumption that regulation is harmful) or on those who want to build it (ie. the company needs to prove their product is safe)?
- Evidence provided by conceptual arguments: Do we treat these as essentially trustworthy if written with a sufficient degree of care and evaluated by folks with good judgement or do we treat them as groundless speculation, at least relative to the null hypothesis or arguments that rely more heavily on empirical results?
- Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of many technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view, in contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish. There’s also a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward).

“AGI”, “human-level intelligence”, “transformative AI”:

I think it’s worth commenting on these terms as they’ll come up during this course:

- If you want to know more about how AGI can be defined, section 2 of the “Levels of AGI” DeepMind paper provides a helpful summary of proposed definitions, though I view their descriptions as missing a lot of context. It is hard to evaluate a definition without knowing the purpose for which it was constructed: Is it trying to capture the ‘essence’ of the concept or merely proposing an operationalisation for a specific study? Are the authors primarily interested in understanding specific kinds of impacts or impacts in general? Have they stated their goal? What other terms is AGI being defined in contrast to? Along these kinds of lines, Ilya argues that the term “AGI” as a goal is a reaction to narrow AI: “Well this is not good. It is so narrow. What we need is general AI, an AI that can just do all the things”. He argues that a human is not an AGI “because a human being lacks a huge amount of knowledge”; ie. that AGI would be beyond human-level intelligence.
- Terms like “AGI” are notoriously slippery. If you adopt a quite broad definition, then you can argue that ChatGPT was an “ early (but still incomplete) version of an artificial general intelligence system ” like Microsoft Research’s 2023 Sparks of AGI paper or that AI is already human-level like a 2026 Nature paper. These views can be supported by arguing AI skeptics often present an unrealistically optimistic picture of human intelligence. Conversely, if your definition of AGI requires it to match humans in essentially every conceivable task, then AGI timelines may end up surprisingly long. After all, it’s hard to rule out the possibility of there being even one obscure task that proves surprisingly hard to automate. The Levels of AGI paper provides a helpful performance × generality matrix (attached), however given that capabilities appear more jagged than the ChatGPT days, I would personally want to add a third column in between narrow and general.

- One of the most famous definitions of AGI (technically whether machines can “think”) is the Turing Test. A 2026 paper by Jones and Bergen observed LLMs (GPT 4.5 and Llama) that were prompted to act like humans successfully passed a three-way Turing test, as per Turing’s original setup, where an interrogator is interviewing two agents: one human and one AI. This setup is more difficult to pass because the interrogator can directly compare the two and because they don’t need to guess the base rate. The interrogators were given 5 minutes (matching the duration mentioned in Turing’s paper, though this was only by way of example, rather a specification). These interrogators were drawn from two subsets: students and a company called Prolific (Turing only spoke of “average” interrogators). Some people have criticised this paper on the basis that some of the interrogators didn’t seem to try that hard. Whilst impressive, it’s worth noting that this kind of linguistic imitation is arguably precisely what LLMs are made for, in which case we should expect their performance here to be much less indicative of their general abilities than if AI had been produced another way.
- In A Definition of AGI (Oct 2025), Hendrycks et al. attempt to define AGI using Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory, “the most empirically validated model of human cognition”. They write, “”AGI is an AI that can match or exceed the cognitive versatility and proficiency of a well-educated adult”. However, whilst this model is verified as providing a robust categorisation of intellectual abilities in humans, it doesn’t automatically mean that these categories are suitable for AI, especially since artificial intelligence is often spiky in ways that feels utterly bizarre to humans.

- Dario isn’t really a fan of the term as he believes there’s no clear boundary between AGI and non-AGI. One analogy I like: if you’re on a road trip from San Fransisco to New York and someone wants to know how long it’ll be, it initially doesn’t matter very much whether you’re headed to New York state or New York city (or which neighbour in New York), but as you get closer, the precise definition becomes much more important. Helen Toner makes more or less the same argument using fuzzy clouds in concept space: “it had a good run”. On the other hand, Sam Altman shares these worries but has resigned himself to the term’s popularity: “the word seems so sticky, I gave up trying to fight it”.

My top recommendation for better understanding where we are now: Honestly, I need to find a new one (I would appreciate suggestions!). I was previously recommending What the hell happened with AGI Timelines in 2026? to my previous cohort, where Rob Wiblin attempted to synthesize a lot of different data into a coherent view:

- For example, he listed “AI does some original math” as ambiguous. OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed. There’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data, but they also dropped 372 other results onto the internet (yet to be verified; some of these have Lean proofs, but it is possible to make a mistake in how a problem is formalised). Frontier Math Tier 4 has also been saturated.
- He also said that time horizons were on trend. Time horizons now appear remarkably above trend (thought these results have been criticised).
- Counterpoint: Toby Ord has argued that inference-time compute scales less favourably than you might expect. Many folk have missed the fact that certain linear seeming graphs actually have a log-scale on the x-axis.

General Trends:

- BlueDot’s 2 hour Future of AI course contains a lot of information on this. I’ve attached a picture showing the progress in image models and a graph showing the amount of money being invested.

- A diagram from Epoch’s Trends in Artificial Intelligence show the current rate of progress of various components of AI

- A frequently cited, but somewhat old, diagram from Our World shows benchmarks saturating increasingly fast. Unfortunately, the benchmark situation seems to have become worse recently.

Scale of Societal Impact:

The Technological Richter Scale: This tools allows you to calibrate the predicted impact of AI against other technologies.

MirrorCode and Emergent Abilities

Fable 5 achieved a substantial advance on MirrorCode (64% vs. 20% for GPT 5.6 Sol), a benchmark involving reimplementing an entire program end-to-end:

- Unfortunately, I haven’t had time to look into this benchmark in detail, but it really made me stop and think because it makes the rapid upwards trend on METR time horizons feel much more plausible to me. The METR time horizons have absurdly large error bars, as well as having been subject to various criticisms; whilst I didn’t necessarily didn’t believe their results, I effectively had them down as a “maybe, who knows” in my mind. Seeing the rapid advance in MirrorCode makes we wonder, “Wait, should I be believing the METR’s most recent results? Because if so, that would be huge!”
- It’s worth noting that the benchmark requires a 100% test pass rate in order to pass an individual task. The fact that it uses such a strongly binary scoring system helps explain how it was possible for progress on this benchmark to take-off so quickly. As Boaz Barak observes, if completing a task really means completing a number of tasks of similar difficulty successfully, then the success curve tends to end up being much steeper.

- This ties directly into the question of emergent abilities: many folks have observed cases where capabilities have rather suddenly emerged as training scaled. However, Schaffer et al have suggested that this is a mirage as the emergence phenomena depends on the specific metric researchers observe.

- Boaz counters that even if there is a metric according to which an ability was just following the trend, this is only helpful if we know that this is the right metric in advance. If we don’t know how to decompose a task into “simpler predictable components”, then we may still experience capability increases as more or less emergent.
- This isn’t just a theoretical question. The capabilities of Mythos seem to have caught many people by surprise (note how quickly the Trump administration swapped from voluntary to “voluntary” evaluation of frontier models). As mentioned in Setting the Scene the graph showing CVEs is wild. Some people expected this, most did not.

- The extent to which the capabilities or impacts of models can be predicted in advance affects the degree to which evals should be central to the way companies and broader society approach the issue of safety. Institutions want to be able to produce legible schemes of regulation as it reduces their reliance of subjective judgement. Sometimes this is possible, other times this only produces false assurance.

Take-off Speeds:

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speed is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018): “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)”. At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips” (from Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me).

Forethought defines an additional scenario: a “bumpy” intelligence explosion. More on this later, but one way this could happen would be if AI progress feeds back into developing better models for a while, but it then becomes bottlenecked (perhaps because the loop is longer for AI to recursively improve the chips we use to run and train it or maybe because we need to fully automate chip production)

Two older definitions (mostly defunct; included for historical reasons):

- Vernor Vinge: Soft = years; hard = “very short period of time”, perhaps less than 100 hours
- Eliezer Yudkowsky: Fast = weeks or hours vs. years or decades

Timelines

It’s worth being aware that when people talk about AI timelines they’re often imagining very different milestones. Given the difficultly of predicting the future, we might not want to be place too much confidence in our predictions:

- I’ve included a table from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lists four potential paths from AGI to ASI (artificial superintelligence).

- Current Metaculus predictions are September 2027 for weakly general AI and Nov 2030 for a stronger definition of general AI to be developed and publicly announced. However, it’s hard to know how much we should trust prediction markets on questions regarding transformative technologies as they haven’t been around for that long (Metaculus was founded in 2015).
- The AI Futures model (an update of the AI 2027 model) currently predicts automated coding around October 2027 (operationalised as an AI that would be as productive on its own as only human coders with no AIs; guidance on research taste is still provided by humans) and superintelligence around December 2028 (defined as the gap between the AI and the best humans is twice the gap between the best humans and the median professional on virtually all cognitive tasks). There forecasts tend to be on the more aggressive side, but less so than their previous work; many frontier lab employees, or other folks in the Bay area, now seem to be expecting similar rates of progress. As of August 2026, they felt that AI was moving at 70-90% of the rate they’d predicted in AI 2027.

- Frontier Lab Predictions: In June 2026, Dario wrote: “If these scaling laws continue for only a year or two longer, we are likely to get what I’ve called Powerful AI, or “a country of geniuses in a datacenter”“. Jack Clark recently declared that the singularity has begun. Time reported that Sam Altman said that OpenAI was “not quite yet” there, but “by the end of the year (2026) the company would have an internal system he would call AGI”. They claim to have already achieved an automated research intern in September of 2026 and that OpenAI has suggested that may be achieve their goal of an automated AI researcher by March of 2028 (defined as “a significant fraction of our research being done by AI systems in tandem with our own researchers”). Demis has described AGI as 2-3 years away. One frustrating aspect of these debates is that frontier lab employees have access to a lot information that outsiders lack. Often they point to these kinds of internal results as the basis of their beliefs (ie. Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI writes, “Based on internal results, I have a strong expectation that this speed of progress could be sustained into recursive self-improvement). I’m glad to see Anthropic and OpenAI making an effort to start sharing some of what they’re seeing internally, but we still have to take much more on faith than would be ideal.

If you’re reading this ahead of time to prepare for a BlueDot course, I also recommend reading Daniel Selsam’s Personal Statement on AI Risk (it is the opener for the latest version of the strategy course, but I recommend this for all courses).

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.
